1. Which of these 4 could be the probability distribution decision of a neural network? _ b
   _
        a. [0,0,0,0]     b. [0,.4,0,.6]       c. [-.5,0,.5,0]     d. [.3,.3,.4,.5]

   Only (b) is possible. The numbers in a probability distribution have to be between 0
   and 1 and all add up to 1. (a) adds up to 0, (c) has a negative number, and (d) adds
   up to 1.5.

2. Name three ways in which we can distinguish consonants from each other.

   Voicing (whether the vocal folds vibrate), place of articulation (where in the mouth
   the sound is made, e.g., labial, dental, alveolar, postalveolar, or velar), manner of
    articulation (how the air is constricted, e.g., fricative, oral stop, or nasal stop), and
    nasality (whether the velum is lowered to allow the air to escape through the nose).
   Any 3 of the four.


3. One side of the basilar membrane is heavy and not stiƯ, while the other side is light and
    very stiƯ. How do these facts enable audition?

   Frequency goes up with stiƯness and down with mass (k↑ f↑, m↑ f↓), so the heavy,
   non-stiƯ end of the membrane vibrates at low frequencies and the light, stiƯ end
    vibrates at high frequencies. Each part is hooked to neurons that tell the brain
   which frequencies they heard based on location.

4. Can you describe how dynamic programming works in terms of the size of problems,
   and problems containing other problems

   You break the big problem into smaller subproblems until you reach small
   problems that are trivial to solve. You solve those smallest problems ﬁrst, then use
    their answers to solve the larger problems that contain them, all the way to the
   hardest problems.


5. Can you describe why dynamic programming is more eƯicient than the exhaustive
   algorithm?


   The paths in a shortest-path problem overlap. The exhaustive algorithm solves
   every path separately, so it redoes the same additions over and over. Dynamic
   programming solves only the non-overlapping parts. It ﬁnds the best solution from
   each state only once and reuses it for every path through that state, so it never
   repeats work.




6. Which of these is “f” as in “family” __ b __ and which is “th” as in “thing” __ a ___





                  aa               bb

    In (b) the lower lip is against the upper teeth (labial); in (a) the tongue tip is up at the
   teeth (dental).


7.  Describe how the Stochastic Gradient Descent Algorithm works in your own words.

  We want to estimate a quantity from some existing data, like the average of a list of
   numbers. We start with a random estimate, pick a random data point, and
   compute the loss (the diƯerence between our guess and that data point). Then we
   subtract a small fraction of the loss (the learning rate) from the guess to get a new,
    slightly better guess. We repeat this with new random data points over and over,
   and the guess gets closer and closer to the real answer.

8. What’s the similarity between “n” in “neck” and “d” in “deck”, and what’s the diƯerence
   between those sounds?
   Both are voiced alveolar stops. The diƯerence is that n is a nasal stop, so the air
   comes out through the nose, while d is an oral stop, so the air is blocked
   completely and then released through the mouth.

9. What’s the similarity and diƯerence between the vowels in “mean” and “moon”?
   Both are high vowels. The diƯerence is that the vowel in “mean” is a front vowel,
   while the vowel in “moon” is a back vowel (lips also rounded).

10. Imagine a Stochastic Gradient Algorithm (SGD) with a very low learning rate and a
   springy system (with no mass) with a low stiƯness. a) Describe how the Estimate of
  SGD and the equilibrium position for the spring system evolve with time. b) How would
   the evolution in time diƯer, if the learning rate and stiƯness increased? For SGD, ignore
    accuracy/oscillation for this question.
    a) Both move toward their goal slowly. With a low learning rate, the SGD estimate
   only takes a small correction toward the average each time, so it takes many steps
   to get there. With low stiƯness, the spring only pulls weakly, so it drifts back to its
   equilibrium position slowly.

    b) Both would get there faster. A higher learning rate makes bigger corrections
   toward the average, and a stiƯer spring pulls harder and snaps back to equilibrium
   more quickly.


11. Describe the psychological principle of closure, illustrated by this ﬁgure           , and
   how is it used in the GPT system as a principle for learning?
  Humans are very adept at ﬁlling in missing information using what we already
   know. In the ﬁgure no triangle is actually drawn, but we see one anyway because
   our brain completes the shape. GPT learns the same way (the cloze task). It takes a
   sentence, pretends a part of a sentence is missing, and asks the network to
   complete what’s missing. If the guess is wrong, the weights get adjusted, and after
    billions of these completions the system ends up “knowing” the language.

  make it. Describe why I put it this way.

20. In SGD for averaging a list, the mathematical formula for the New Estimate of average x
     is: New x = Current x – lr (Current x – data point d to learn from). And lr is the learning
    rate. What is the purpose of the ﬁrst minus in the formula?

   The minus makes the estimate move toward the data point regardless if the data is
   above or below the true estimate. If the estimate is above the data point, the loss is
    positive, so subtracting it pushes the estimate down. If the estimate is below the
   data point, the loss is negative, so subtracting it pushes the estimate up.
